doc.title: Ada Rovatti interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 13, 2022

title: Telling a story and engaging the audience
summary: She wants jazz to interact with the audience rather than be a private conversation; cueing the band on solos.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: I like that, you have something to say. I know that some of the older generation of musicians they used to say well tell a story when you’re improvising.

Yeah but I think it’s the same the moment we are talking me and you right now is an exchange of question and comments and a little comedy, a little — and the same should be on the bandstand it’s just an interaction and you want to be sure that not only the musician gets the interaction but also the audience. I was actually talking today, I was in the car with Randy and saying that sometimes some of the jazz that I hear it sounds like a private conversation between elite musicians. And you know you cannot remember any melody or any — you just don’t — I mean I do appreciate that that kind of intellect for music because it’s really kind of like intellectual and can — but you know what about the famous music is entertainment? You have also the audience be part of it. If it’s just a private talk between just elite musicians, that’s bad. So I like to hear the melody, I like that people can just move their head, they just kind of you see that they have a feedback. That’s how I get excited and I play better. You know? If it’s just between me and my music and a couple of my friends we can just stay in the basement and we’ll do the same.

I liked watching, there’s a number of videos on YouTube of you in the Brecker Brothers and there’s one moment where you’re taking sort of an extended solo and I mean this is not a big deal, it’s bandstand etiquette, but you turn and you give the band a cue.
Like okay let’s move — like I’m done — and then the band moves on. I just love that stuff. And I think people who are in the audience who are really into it, they probably see that.
Yeah I think so, plus I’m Italian, I’m always moving my hands. You know the joke how do you shut up an Italian? You tie their hands behind their back. So I do very good on the stage.
